did_you_know.text: The title attributes the psalm to the Sons of Korah and describes it as a “maskil.” The title itself highlights its connection to a tradition of song and instruction.
The psalmist uses the image of a deer thirsting for water to express the intensity of his longing for God: just as the deer longs for water, so his soul longs for the Lord.
This verse contains several expressions of spiritual longing: “My soul thirsts,” “for God,” and “for the living God.” This longing is also described as a desire to come and appear before God.
The psalmist describes his tears as his “bread,” meaning that they accompany him day and night. Alongside his pain, the taunt of those around him keeps returning: “Where is your God?”
The memory takes the psalmist back to his pilgrimage to the house of God. He remembers going among the crowd, amid joyful singing, thanksgiving, and communal celebration.
The psalm presents an inner conversation: the psalmist asks his soul why it is downcast, and immediately encourages it to hope in God and look forward to giving thanks again for salvation.
The image “deep calls to deep,” together with the references to waves and breakers, describes the intensity of the turmoil the psalmist is experiencing through pictures of raging waters.
Alongside his distress, the psalmist expresses faith in enduring love: by day the Lord commands his steadfast love, and by night the psalmist responds with prayer and a song to the living God.
The psalmist addresses God as “my Rock,” emphasizing an image of stability and refuge, even as he continues to ask why he feels forgotten and is oppressed by his enemies.
The final verse again calls the soul to hope in God. Repeating the central idea gives the psalm an ending marked by hope, future thanksgiving, and expectation of salvation.
